summary: An accident happens between boarding with the intention of flight and everyone getting off, when someone is killed or seriously injured by the aircraft (including parts that fall off, and jet blast), when the aircraft suffers structural damage needing major repair (damage only to the engine, propeller, wingtips, aerials, tyres, brakes or small dents doesn't count), or when it is missing. The commander tells the AAIB (Chief Inspector of Air Accidents) and the police by the quickest means. The State where it happens investigates, to find the cause and prevent a repeat, never to blame. Report all bird strikes, and MORs through the CAA's portal.
sections: What counts as an accident
An occurrence between the time anyone boards with the intention of flight and the time all have left, in which:

– someone is killed or seriously injured: in or on the aircraft, by direct contact with any part of it (including parts that have come off), or by jet blast. Not if from natural causes, self-inflicted, inflicted by others, or a stowaway outside the normal areas.

– the aircraft has damage or structural failure that affects its strength, performance or flight characteristics and would normally need major repair or replacement. Not an accident: damage limited to the engine, its cowlings or accessories; or to propellers, wingtips, aerials, tyres, brakes, fairings, small dents or punctures.
– the aircraft is missing or completely inaccessible (missing = the official search has ended without finding the wreckage).

Exam trap A person on the ground hit by a part that fell off an aircraft in flight → accident. A person on the apron hit by the wingtip of a taxiing aircraft → accident (someone boarded with the intention of flight).
Serious injury
Hospital for more than 48 hours, starting within 7 days
a fracture (except simple fractures of fingers, toes or nose)
lacerations causing severe bleeding or nerve, muscle or tendon damage
injury to an internal organ
second or third-degree burns, or burns over 5% of the body
verified exposure to infectious substances or harmful radiation
Notifying an accident
The commander (or the operator if the commander is killed or incapacitated) tells, by the quickest means:
– the Chief Inspector of Air Accidents (the AAIB)
– the local police, if it happened in or over the UK
The State in which the accident happens starts the investigation.
Incidents

An occurrence, other than an accident, that affected or could have affected safety. Examples: an Airprox, a near miss with the ground, undershooting or overshooting a runway, a structural or engine failure that isn't an accident, crew incapacitation, low fuel leading to a Mayday.
Serious incident: one that almost resulted in an accident. Damage or injury = accident; could have = incident.
Purpose of an investigation
Only to find the cause and prevent recurrence. Investigators do not apportion blame or liability.
The commander must assist the investigators.
The CAA is legally responsible for implementing safety recommendations.
CHIRP (the Confidential Human Factors Incident Reporting Programme) takes confidential reports; its GA Feedback is published online.
ICAO Annex 13
Procedures for States investigating accidents and incidents, so experts from different States cooperate and the lessons are shared worldwide.
An accredited investigator may: visit the scene, examine the wreckage, get witness information, have access to all relevant evidence, take part in tests and simulations, and make submissions.
Reporting
Bird strikes: report all of them, damage or not. Near misses are welcome too.
Mandatory Occurrence Reports (MOR): the events listed in Regulation 2015/1018 (under Regulation 376/2014). Anything else can go in as a voluntary report.
The book gives the EU's online portal; UK pilots report to the CAA through its own online occurrence-reporting portal (check the CAA website for the current link).

sum.What counts as an accident: Death or serious injury, structural damage needing major repair, or a missing aircraft, between boarding and everyone getting off.
sum.Serious injury: Over 48 hours in hospital, most fractures, serious cuts, organ damage, bad burns, infection or radiation.
sum.Notifying an accident: Commander tells the AAIB and the police by the quickest means; the State of Occurrence investigates.
sum.Incidents: Anything else that affected or could have affected safety; a serious incident almost became an accident.
sum.Purpose of an investigation: To find the cause and prevent recurrence, not to blame; the commander must help.
sum.ICAO Annex 13: How States investigate and share the lessons.
sum.Reporting: Report every bird strike; MORs and voluntary reports go to the CAA online.

cards.q: When does the accident 'window' start and end?
cards.a: From when anyone boards with the intention of flight until all have left.

cards.q: Is a person on the ground hit by a part that fell off an aircraft an accident?
Is damage limited to the propeller an accident?
cards.a: No (nor engine-only damage, wingtips, aerials, tyres, brakes, small dents).

cards.q: Is a missing aircraft an accident?
cards.a: Yes, once the official search ends without finding the wreckage.

cards.q: Who must be told of a UK accident, and how?
cards.a: The Chief Inspector of Air Accidents (AAIB) and the local police, by the quickest means.

cards.q: Who tells them if the commander is killed?

cards.a: The State in which the accident happens.
To find the cause and prevent recurrence; not to apportion blame or liability.
More than 48 hours, starting within 7 days.

cards.q: Which fractures don't count as serious injury?
cards.a: Simple fractures of fingers, toes or nose.
An accident has the damage or injury; a serious incident nearly did.

cards.q: Which bird strikes must be reported?
cards.a: All of them, damage or not.
Confidential Human Factors Incident Reporting Programme.

quiz.q: Which of these is an aircraft accident?
o: A person on the ground is seriously injured by a part that falls off an aircraft in flight
A tyre bursts on landing and the aircraft has to be towed clear of the runway
An aerial breaks off in flight and is found later beside the runway
A bird strike in flight leaves a small dent in the wing leading edge
quiz.why: Injury from a detached part is an accident. Tyres, aerials and small dents are listed exceptions.

quiz.q: An engine fails in the circuit and the aircraft lands safely on the runway. Damage is limited to the engine. This is:
o: Not an accident; engine-only damage is excluded
An accident
A serious injury occurrence
An accident only if the engine must be replaced
quiz.why: Damage limited to the engine, its cowlings or accessories is excluded. It is still reportable as an occurrence.

quiz.q: A person on the apron is seriously injured by the wingtip of an aircraft taxiing for departure. This is:
o: An accident
An incident
Not reportable
An accident only if the aircraft is damaged
quiz.why: People had boarded with the intention of flight, and a person was seriously injured by direct contact with the aircraft.

quiz.q: A UK accident must be reported by the quickest means to:
o: The Chief Inspector of Air Accidents and the local police
The CAA and the Chief Inspector of Air Accidents
The CAA and the local police where it happened
The aircraft's operator and its insurer
quiz.why: AAIB (the Chief Inspector) and the police. The CAA is the trap.

quiz.q: Who is responsible for starting the investigation of an accident?
o: The authority of the State in which it occurred
The authority of the State of Registry
The CAA, wherever in the world it happens
The aircraft's operator, with the insurer
quiz.why: The State of Occurrence starts the investigation; other States may take part.

quiz.q: The purpose of an accident investigation is to:
o: Find the cause and prevent recurrence
Decide who was to blame
Assess liability for insurers
Decide whether to prosecute the pilot
quiz.why: Investigators do not apportion blame or liability.

quiz.q: Which of these counts as a serious injury?
o: A broken arm
A simple fracture of a finger
A night in hospital for observation
A small cut
quiz.why: Most fractures count, but not simple fractures of fingers, toes or nose. Hospital must be more than 48 hours.

quiz.q: Which bird strikes should be reported?
o: All of them, whether or not there is damage
Only those that cause damage to the aircraft
Only those that lead to an accident or injury
Only those at aerodromes with an ATC unit
quiz.why: Every bird strike, and near misses are welcome too.
